result_scope: arm A2 only. Arm A1 is suspended in none of the runs, and is documented as beyond the reach of any response gated on an audit record - its process lives 230-383 ms against a 600-1010 ms delivery lag. The criterion asks for *a* third-party encryptor and A2 meets it repeatably; A1 is an arm this project added beyond it. Both are reported in full below and neither bound was moved.

criterion.attack: third-party encryptor suspended within 20 files and under 2 s
criterion.benign: ffmpeg transcode, 7-Zip archive and git clone complete untouched
criterion.unchanged_since: the run that failed it; neither bound was moved

_read_the_result_with_this: The criterion asks for *a* third-party encryptor suspended inside two bounds. Arm A2 - a loop around openssl enc, one process per file - meets both in 6 of 6 replicates, with the worst run at 18 files and 1.215 s. Arm A1, 7-Zip with -sdel, is suspended in none of them, and it is not a near miss: the process lives 230-383 ms and the audit record that names it takes 600-1010 ms to arrive, so it has exited before any attribution-gated response can act. That is a property of the mechanism - LIMITATIONS sections 1 and 4 - and not a threshold somebody could tune. A1 is run because this project chose to run it, not because the criterion asked for two shapes. A reader who takes PASSED to mean 'this stops ransomware' has taken more than the evidence supports; see _what_this_does_not_show.

attack_arms.arm: A2 openssl enc -aes-256-cbc (one process per file)
attack_arms.why_replicated: The response cannot land before the Security channel flushes the record naming the writer, and that flush is a periodic timer of about a second. Where the attack's first write falls inside that interval is arbitrary and moves FEBR by more than the whole width of the bound, so one run measures one draw. The spread above is the distribution, not a headline.
attack_arms.how_it_is_caught: Not by the process that writes the ciphertext. Each openssl lives about 65 ms against roughly 1000 ms of delivery lag and is long gone before it can be named. What is caught is the loop's driver, which unlinks each original - a long-lived process, named through the DELETE access right, on the first decoy it removes. The decoys sort to the front of the directory, so the tripwire fires about 60 ms into the attack and everything after that is waiting for Windows.

attack_arms.arm: A1 7z a -p -mhe=on -mx=0 -sdel over the whole directory
attack_arms.verdict: FAIL - nothing suspended, the whole corpus destroyed
attack_arms.why_it_is_missed: One number. 7-Zip archives and unlinks five hundred 100 KB documents in 383.2 ms at 124.3 MB/s (reports/encryptor_lifetime.json), and the audit record that names it arrives 600-1010 ms after the write. Everything upstream of the response worked: the decoy tripwire fired 118 ms in, the agent resolved the deletions to 7z.exe with CERTAIN confidence and logged it, and the response was refused with 'the response guard refused pid 29172: PID 29172 does not exist'. Detection is not the binding constraint here and neither is the correlation window; the process is simply gone.
attack_arms.two_earlier_explanations_that_were_wrong: This artefact previously said that -sdel unlinks only after the archive completes, and attributed the miss to the container-separability result. The first came from a harness that sampled the file count only when the set of live PIDs changed, which for a one-process arm means twice; the first unlink is actually about 130 ms in. The second is a real limitation (LIMITATIONS section 6) that does not bite here, because the decoy field does not consult the entropy verdict and it fired correctly. See CORRECTIONS.md correction 10.

control_did_the_harness_change_do_this._why: One harness change between the failing run and this one helps the agent: the arms now wait until the agent's own ledger stops growing (13.2-13.6 s) instead of sleeping a fixed 12 s, so the attack no longer starts while the agent is still draining the five hundred files it was just given. Removing that confound is right - nobody creates a corpus twelve seconds before being attacked - but it is still a change in the agent's favour, and a result that rested on it would have to say so. These replicates force the old fixed sleep back on and change nothing else.
control_did_the_harness_change_do_this.finding: The pass does not depend on it. With the old fixed 12 s sleep, FEBR is [10, 17, 16] - still inside the bound of 20. The settle change removes a confound; it does not produce the result.

benign_arms.not_run: ffmpeg is not installed on this host. The arm is named in the brief and is reported as not run rather than substituted with a different tool.

benign_verdict: PASS on the three arms that ran, and this pass carries weight on two counts. The same build in the same session suspended arm A2 on a certain attribution, so the detector was capable of acting. And each arm now outlives the audit delivery lag, so a response could have reached it - in the previous run B1, B2 and B3 finished in 0.13 s, 0.43 s and 0.12 s, all shorter than the lag, and 'completed untouched' was true of them whatever the detector decided. ffmpeg is not installed on this host and is reported as not run rather than substituted. Arms still too short to be conclusive: ['B2 git clone (full history, no hardlinks)'].

what_changed_since_the_failing_run.the_decoys_jump_the_queue: Each lane now serves a priority queue first, and a canary event is the only thing that goes in it. In the failing run five events were parked and none were resolved by re-asking - every other one reached its lane after the record explaining it had already arrived, because the queue was more than a second behind. A tripwire wired through a backlog is not a tripwire.
what_changed_since_the_failing_run.the_protection_path_no_longer_reads_the_: The per-path baseline lookup ran get_blocks(file_path=...), which is a leading-wildcard LIKE over the event_data JSON - a full scan of the chain, twice, with no index that can serve it - on a lane, on the one SQLite connection the fan-out thread was writing through. 4.4 ms at 3300 blocks against 2.5 ms for the whole of detection, growing with the chain, and paid for every path the agent had not seen before. It is now one indexed query at startup (966 baselines in 10.1 ms) and a dict lookup at 0.09 us thereafter, kept current from the agent's own writes.
what_changed_since_the_failing_run.the_response_guard_stopped_walking_the_p: psutil.Process().parents() measured 81 ms median, 100 ms max - against 0.01 ms for every other call in guard() including the suspend itself. It was the entire agent-side cost of a response and was paid on every one, including each response later refused because the PID had exited. Cached for five seconds, with getpid and getppid still read every call. guard() went from 88 ms to 0.013 ms.
what_changed_since_the_failing_run.measured_effect: FEBR 37 in the failing run; median 20.5 with the first two fixes; median 17.5 and worst case 18 with all three.

the_floor_under_all_of_this.rule: FEBR >= the audit delivery lag x the attacker's write rate
the_floor_under_all_of_this.worked: At 16.5 files/s a delivery lag of 0.6-1.0 s costs 10-17 documents before any response is physically possible. The measured range is 10-18. The agent's own share is what is left: from the moment it has a CERTAIN attribution to the moment the process is frozen is now single-digit milliseconds.
the_floor_under_all_of_this.what_would_close_it: Only a mechanism that names the writer synchronously with the write - a filesystem minifilter, kernel-mode code requiring a signing certificate Microsoft issues to registered vendors. See LIMITATIONS section 1. Widening any threshold here would change the reported number without changing the number of files the attacker actually got.

_what_this_does_not_show: That the agent stops ransomware. It shows that one of two third-party encryptor shapes is suspended mid-campaign, repeatably, inside both bounds, with a measured loss and a measured time; that the other is beyond the reach of any response gated on an audit record, for a reason measured in reports/encryptor_lifetime.json; and that three benign tools doing real work ran untouched in a configuration that was demonstrably capable of suspending something.
